utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Anna Richterova and Julian Nicholls for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, along with my co-counsel Milan Trbojevic and our assistant Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you too. How are you, sir? Are you better -- feeling better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Yes. Thank you. I'm feeling quite well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. May I ask you to stand up so that you enter the same solemn declaration as you did yesterday and then we can proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And you may sit down. Now, take my advice, because I was noticing you yesterday -- it's true that you were sitting there in the same chair answering questions being fired to you first from the Prosecution then from the Defence. And I know this is -- this is an experience with which you are not familiar and which is tiring. Take it easy. I mean, relax -- keep relaxed and calm as much as you can. Try to understand the question. I emphasise once more the importance of leaving a little bit of time before you answer, so that you make the life of the interpreters a little bit less difficult than it was yesterday. And then leave the rest to us. Mr. Zecevic, can I ask you to come forward like you did yesterday, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honours. I have already prepared over here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that. Thank you. And you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we broke with the time when you left the sports hall. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you spent about seven days in that sports hall. The guards were Serb policemen, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Wearing blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Two or three days after you left to go to the house of your friend you said that military policemen came to fetch you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, military policemen came with a vehicle of the Niva brand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony here in the Tribunal you said that you concluded they were military policemen because they were wearing uniforms and had white belts. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, military policemen wearing white belts. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, this vehicle, Lada Niva was it painted in a particular colour?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a civilian vehicle, a Lada that used to be used before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So it was not a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was as I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Those persons took you to the SUP, as you said, for an information interview; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They took me to the SUP for an information interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When they brought you to the SUP, they handed you over to the inspector by the name of Zoric.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left me in the corridor to wait there, and the inspector came and took me to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So they were not present while you were making your statement to Inspector Zoric and then to Inspector Sobot.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These gentlemen, Zoric and Sobot, were police inspectors before, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They used to work in the police before too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that during your interrogation they did not use physical force against you, either of them.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only Zoric shouted at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The questions they put to you had to do with your knowledge about any weapons and whether you possessed any weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony yesterday while being examined by my learned friend the Prosecutor, you said that you didn't know anything about these things because in those days you were preoccupied with the construction of your house. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I had just started a family then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, did you have any knowledge of the purchase of illegal weapons on a large scale in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no knowledge about any such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know, because you worked in the court, that possession of illegal weapons was a crime according to the law in force at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't follow the law because I was an ordinary employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, the translation said, "I didn't follow the law because I was an ordinary employee." I would imagine that what you mean is that you did not study law or did not take an interest in the law. Correct? Because it could also mean that you didn't follow the law -- that you did not observe it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't study the law. I just completed an ordinary secondary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, I brought this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. But in our language, it's -- it's very clearly distinctive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's why I didn't intervene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me please, after you made that statement you said the interrogation went on for four or five hours, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were then taken to the elementary school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the gym of the elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then the next day you were transferred to the Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, in Betonirka you were put up in a garage. And in the statement that you gave to the investigator in 2001 you said that the detainees were brought there and taken away by Macura and Dosenovic, the policemen.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just make a pause because of the interpreters, please. In the Betonirka reserve policemen were also on guard duty, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Martic, Cetkovic, Kravic as shift leaders; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cetkovic was a shift leader, and so was Martic. But Kravic was a guard in the shift of which the leader was Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All three persons were also police officers, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean were they part of the reserve police force or not?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They wore the uniforms of reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday while testifying here in court, on page 30, line 5 to 8 of the LiveNote, that you were beaten in Betonirka simply because you were a member of the Muslim nation.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that they slapped you only once during that whole 30-day period that you spent in Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Martic did that, the shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So with the exception of that slap, they didn't beat you even though you were a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were other kinds of mistreatment in Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a difference in the way the prisoners were beaten?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no difference between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you is whether some detainees were beaten more frequently than others.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Commander Burnic, didn't you, in that context?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention Commander Burnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned him, saying that he was beaten up particularly frequently; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this Mr. Burnic was a police commander before, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Martic, who was shift leader, he was also a policeman before.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that gentleman Mr. Martic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't know whether Mr. Martic used to work as an active-duty policeman before.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know him until I was brought to Betonirka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that occasionally you would go to the kitchen and bring food for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an order in which people went to fetch food together with the guards. When we were told to go, we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So was this a large kitchen?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military kitchen accommodated in the yard of the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that kitchen was used to feed the soldiers as well as the prisoners, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was used for preparing food.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP in 2001 on page 7, third paragraph, you said that the kitchen was used to feed many of us, both the detainees and the Serbs [As interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we prisoners and soldiers. I saw them when I went there to get food.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of July, 1992 you were taken out of the garage, and you said that a policeman, a certain Veselinovic, put a knife to your neck.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that your name was first on the list of the people to be transported to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what the guard told me when I asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, you told us yesterday that there were about 60 of you who got onto that truck.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Jakov Maric among those 60 people, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember. He was a Croat from Sasina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And he was in the same truck as you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us yesterday that as you arrived in front of the Manjaca camp, when they lifted the tarpaulin the leader of the convoy and the deputy commander of the camp who came out realised that about 18 people had died of suffocation in the truck.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that escorting the convoy was the police. That's right, isn't it? I think you mentioned Dosenovic.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the reserve police force. He was the leader of the convoy, because before the war Dragan Dosenovic, also known as Maca, was an active-duty policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that the deputy commander who you saw on that occasion had the nickname Spaga; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how they called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the truck was opened and you got down, Spaga ordered you to carry out the dead from the truck, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The dead and a couple of men who were still showing signs of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 2001 given to the OTP you said that he also said that you should take a pen and paper -- that a pen and paper should be taken and the names of the dead written down.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you write those names down?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Someone else did who knew them better, because there were people from the villages. I only knew the people from downtown Sanski Most, from Mahala and Muhici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know somebody called Mirhad Delic?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in Betonirka for the first time. He was a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was one of the casualties, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This deputy camp commander then ordered you to get water to try and bring them back to life.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He gave us a container with water in an attempt to assist them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Make a pause please because of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You went on to say that the deputy camp commander refused to take in the dead people and instructed those who were escorting the convoy to drive those men back to Sanski Most, telling them that the dead people were their problem; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He said, "We will only accept those who are standing on their two feet." As for the others, he said what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you entered Manjaca on the 7th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the evening. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on that same day, when this tragedy occurred with these men on the truck.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A week later you were registered by the International Red Cross, around the 14th of July; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, my learned friend the Prosecutor has already asked you whether the conditions in Manjaca were significantly better than those in Betonirka. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. They were no better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was more space, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was more room, but there were more men too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But there was more air, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you said yesterday that from time to time during that first week of your stay in Manjaca they beat some ordinary civilians. You told us that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They went in groups of 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But they never beat you, did they?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't called out. Because we had come from Betonirka, they said they didn't need to interrogate us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, those men who were beaten up were beaten up during their interrogations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during their interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that in your statement you said that those interrogations were conducted by these same inspectors, Sobot and others, police inspectors.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, police inspectors who had come from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, the personnel in the camp, the guards, were they fed from the same canteen as you were during your stay in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't notice, because we went to have lunch. As soon as we finished, we had to go back to the stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were several canteens or only one for one part of the camp?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first the kitchen was in the first canteen, and then later a second canteen was formed in the other camp, when the detainees were brought over from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in two parts of the camp there were altogether two kitchens.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, after you left the Manjaca camp, did you draw up a list of the prisoners from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't do any such things. When I met, I had to join up with my family after 19 months -- 15 months. I hadn't seen my son or my wife for 15 months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question, Your Honour, line 14, the witness did answer. I distinctly heard him say "da". You might check with the witness to be sure, but I'm quite certain he did answer. He answered with a yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ackerman. That is right, Your Honours. He did answer, but the answer is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Ackerman. Let's clarify it this way: Sir, when you were asked about how many kitchens there were in the camp, did I hear you well saying that initially there was one kitchen in the first camp and then later on when more prisoners were brought forward from Omarska, a second kitchen was created in a second camp; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is quite correct, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to have interrupted you like, this but I think it was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, something is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not -- wait a minute, because we are not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone wasn't switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says he didn't see his wife for 19 and 15 months, but he said 9 to 10. It says 15 months, but it says 10. Nobody is reacting to the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Here it says, "No, I didn't. I didn't do any such things. When I met, I had to join up with my family after 19 months -- 15 months. I hadn't seen my son or my wife for 15 months. This is what we have here. So what did you actually say? How long had you not seen your wife and your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nine to ten months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nine to ten months. Yes. Thank you. I mean, it's -- when things are -- I am not in a position to know because I don't understand the language. I am getting a few words here and there, but -- but I haven't perfected it as yet. So yes, that goes for the record,. And you may proceed now. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Brdjanin, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me please, Mr. Delic, you returned to Sanski Most in 1997.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of April, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in September of that year, that is, 1997, that you were a party to proceedings in the municipal court?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I started doing my old -- I took up my old job again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were a party in proceedings before the Trial Chamber chaired by Edina Ridjesic, on the 30th of September, 1997, the proclamation of a missing person as being dead, regarding the late Mirko Delic?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that. That is true. That was those proceedings. But you didn't explain what kind of proceedings you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you did take part in those proceedings as a witness, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As a witness who was to testify regarding the date of the death of the late Mirhad Delic.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. I just have a question about the translation line 20. I think this might have been part of the confusion. Counsel's first question is stated "as a party" and then later witness. So I don't know if that translation was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, he wasn't a party for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't my question as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But it's clear -- it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Any question was: Did he took part in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, it was translated whether he was a party. And -- you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown, please, DT22. Could you put the translation on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also -- one of you could clarify this -- because now you referred to this dead person as Mirko Delic. Before you referred to him as Mirhat Delic. In this document he's referred to as Mirhat Delic. And in this statement to the OTP he refers to him as Mirhad. Now, I don't know whether there is any difference between Mirko, Mirhad, Mirhat. Perhaps you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Because we want to make sure that we are talking of the same person in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, the deceased, Mr. Delic, was his name Mirhat or Mirhad?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Delic Mirhad. I met him for the first time, but his name was Mirhad Delic and he originally came from Sandzak. I met him then for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is the last letter "T" or "D" of his first name?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know how it is recorded. I know that his name was Mirhad. It could be a mistake. I know that his surname was Delic and that he was a Muslim by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You see what it says in this ruling. In your opinion to the best of your knowledge, is that his proper name?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Delic Mirhad or Mirhad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And his wife's name is Gospa, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met the lady for the first time. I didn't know her real name because she lived in a different part of town, and originally she came from Lukavica or Fajtovci, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is obvious that the witness does not really know whether it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Janu is pointing out to me, rightly so, that in the text of the decision -- of the decision of the municipal court in Sanski Most, of that -- of the 30th September, there is a marriage to a certificate that was produced during the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we could leave it at that. I just wanted to make sure that when you said Mirko, you were referring to this Mirhad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, this ruling, you've seen it now, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm seeing it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see it before?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After one's testimony the judge draws up the ruling. You don't have to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you told us that you took part in those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that in the ruling it says that the death is being established of Mirhad Delic, the date being the 13th of July, 1992 on the way to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I looked and that is not correct. It should be the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see on page 2 of the English translation, second paragraph, last sentence -- and in the ruling before you it is the second paragraph, again the last sentence, and it says: "The witness, Bekir Delic, said that he had been in a truck with other Muslims on the 13th of July, 1992 when they were transferred to the Manjaca camp and that he had seen Mirhad Delic die of lack of oxygen and water." Is that what you said in court or not?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is not correct, but everything else is true. He was with me in the truck and he passed away. The date is the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that you told the Court that this occurred on the 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I cannot forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know, since you worked in a court, that the date of somebody's death is very important.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One has to know exactly when a certain person died.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me. The witness has already stated that he did not go to law school and what his job at the court was. And I think he's explained that he hadn't seen this order before, he didn't write this order. As far as he knows, a mistake about the date was made following his testimony. I think he's answered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he's volunteered an answer nonetheless. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Delic. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you are now going to be cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm glad you're feeling better today.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not going to take very much of your time. I've just got just a few questions, and I think we'll get through it rather quickly. I'm going to try to ask you questions as much as I can that will be real easy for you to answer with either a yes or a no, because that will get us finished quicker. So if you can, just tell me yes or no when I ask you a question. And if you need to explain something, then, you know, please understand you're free to do that. Before the war, you told us that you worked as a summons server and as a driver; correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For a short time I was a driver, and then I became a court server.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the people you worked for in that regard would have been Judge Adil Draganovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did you last talk to Judge Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last time I saw him was on May 15th, 1992 in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You haven't seen him for ten years.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Now he is the Presiding Judge, the President of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. My question is: When did you last see him? Did you see him last week?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was working. I go to work every morning, and I'm there at 7.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For some reason I'm not making myself clear to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me put the question, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Delic, what we want to know from you, following the question by Mr. Ackerman, is that you now have gone back to Sanski Most and work in the same court building where President Adil Draganovic works. What Mr. Ackerman wants to know is starting from today, when did you last see Judge Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last Friday. So a week ago, exactly a week ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Before I left for here. In the court building, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hand him back to you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity either that day or some day prior to that to discuss with Judge Draganovic the fact that you were coming here and the testimony you were going to give?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only told him that I was -- I would be leaving on June 28th to The Hague so that I could get permission to leave to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did he give you any kind of advice about being a witness here?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't discuss the matter with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know that he had been a witness here?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him on television. There was a short clip from The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall the nature of that clip, what that clip was about?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was very short. When I got into the house, my mother and wife told me, and they just said, "Your president has just been on television."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you didn't actually see it yourself.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't watch television late because I have to get up early, since I'm a server and I have to travel 10 or 15 kilometres to my workplace and I have to be fresh for the day -- the work day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know Zijad Ibric?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He works in the AID.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did you last talk with him? When was the last time you talked with Mr. Ibric?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He saw us off with the gentlemen who came -- a gentleman from the UN who came to fetch us at quarter to 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He saw you off from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He called the driver to come for us, who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you discuss with him anything about the testimony that you would give here?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only saw him officially. But privately, not. I didn't contact him privately at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But when you say you saw him officially, officially did you and he have a conversation about the nature of your testimony in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was only a contact person and informed me about my trip and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 54 of the LiveNote yesterday, sir, you'll recall there was some questioning by Mr. Zecevic of you about uniforms worn by the SOS and specifically camouflage uniforms worn by the SOS. And your answer to

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC WAS
utterances.text: "They wore camouflage uniforms." And then you said this: "And other witnesses can confirm this." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. He asked me, and I just told him about uniforms. The 6th Krajina Brigade soldiers had warm uniforms and the others had light summer uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the part that I'm interested in was when you said, "Other witnesses can confirm this." I'm wondering when you had the opportunity to speak with other witnesses about what they might be able to confirm, if you did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Let me hear you first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just that is -- could be a complete mischaracterisation of what this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could be. In fact, I'm going to ask -- I'm going to stop you, because I fully agree, and I'm going to ask Mr. Ackerman to rephrase the question, in a sense asking the witness whether when he said "Other witnesses can confirm this," he meant that he had discussed the matter with other specific persons that could be brought forward as witnesses and confirm this or that are intended to come forward as witnesses and confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the simple way to ask the question, Your Honour, is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who are the other people that you discussed this with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But that's presuming that he has discussed it with other people. I am pretty sure that what he meant by his statement was that this is something that not just him but even others can come forward and confirm. It doesn't mean to say that he has discussed it with others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is -- and therefore, please first put that kind of question and then move to the second, if it's the case of moving to the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you discuss this issue with other people?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What causes you to conclude that other people can confirm what you told us?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Witnesses that should come and that come -- should come to testify if they have been informed of the same and if they were aware of the distinction between the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, and also in your testimony here yesterday, you told us that Vlado Vrkes represented to you in a meeting that he was some kind of an authority with the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was on May 15th, when they took over the municipal court in Sanski Most, and he introduced himself as Vlado Vrkes and that he was representing the Autonomous District of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said there were about 40 people there, including Judge Adil Draganovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all those -- the employees of the court were there in the court in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Among those being judge -- Judge Draganovic; right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was president of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is not what he was but whether he was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did you learn, if you ever did learn, that -- that it was not true that Vlado Vrkes represented the Autonomous Region of Krajina? Did you ever learn that that was not a true statement?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't find that out ever. I was not into politics. I just heard about it on May 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, that what he told you was that he was representing the regional board of the SDS and not the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know those notions. I'm not an expert. I'm not politically educated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that there was no resistance in Mahala, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then you told us about a time when several -- when you and several other people were escorted by members of the SOS through and from Mahala to the Montenegro Cafe. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From halfway to Mahala. They came to -- halfway to Mahala, and then they were taken back to the cellar that I mentioned, where there was -- drinks were served.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were in that group, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father, mother, family, children, old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I asked you if you were in that group. That's all I asked you. Were you in that group?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I ask the Prosecutor to give you a copy of your statement so that you can look at a part of it with me. If you look on page 4. Sir, it's about two-thirds of the way down. The paragraph begins with the words "Srpski SOS." I believe that's the paragraph I want to refer to. And I think in that paragraph you say this: "My brother, Jasmin Delic, and a young Muslim man were called out and placed in front of their transporter vehicle and used as a human shield as we were escorted through Mahala." That's what it says, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were taken to the cellar, and my brother remained with them, and there was no need for a shield. We were separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you see that language in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor that I just read?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question to you is: Is that what it says in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor? Does it say: "My brother, Jasmin Delic, and a young Muslim man were called out and placed in front of their transporter vehicle and used as a human shield was we were escorted through Mahala"? Does it say that?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While they were taking us. It is said: "They called my brother, Jasmin Delic, and a young Muslim and they put us in front of the transporter vehicle and used as a human shield as we were being escorted through Mahala." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So are you telling us today that you did not tell the Prosecutor that?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. That what is written here in my statement, that's what I told the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you stand by it today as being the truth?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said it, as it has been written. I didn't quite see what was written underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the next day, after you'd spent a night in the basement of that cafe, you told us the cafe owner called the Crisis Staff and asked the Crisis Staff what should be done with the 40 or so of you that were in that basement. That's true; yes?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then after that call to the Crisis Staff, according to your statement to the OTP, a Serb guard told you that you could leave.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he told us that. And then he withdrew into the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. When you were in Betonirka, there were various shifts of guards that worked there; correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who was the shift leader, if you recall, of the -- the guard shift that was very kind to the prisoners, that would leave the doors open and give you extra water and things like that? Who was the shift leader of that shift?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shift leader, Korica Uros -- Uros Korica was his name, if you're referring to him. His name was Uros Korica, the shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I got not interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpretation is coming through. I mean, if you have a technical problem, we'll -- we'll try and fix that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has stopped working, Your Honour. I don't hear anything. Will somebody talk to me. Nothing is happening.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It just came back. Yeah, okay. Try it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpretation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to go to another device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It should be on 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was on 4. It was working fine for a while. I must have dropped something on it. Do you want to talk to me now and see if I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Okay. Now, we got down to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you asked the witness for the name of the leader or shift leader --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And he gave the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- who was kind to the detainees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. In your testimony yesterday, sir, you told us that the SOS carried out the orders of the SDS party. Do you recall telling us that?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Its unit was called the Serbian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever see any written orders from the SDS to the SOS?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anyone from SDS giving orders to the SOS?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no occasion to hear that. I was closed, I was detained, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us about the trip to Manjaca from Betonirka. You said it took about nine hours. Could you tell us how far it is from Betonirka to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It is towards Mrkonjic. I really don't know the area and I had never been there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you accept that it's probably not more than about 70 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know much about roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the witness did not say yesterday the truck was in motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm fully aware of that. I'm coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you spent six hours, I think, sitting at -- at the Krings facility; correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I never mentioned Krings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where was it? Oh, it was the sports hall, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in front of the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you couldn't look out, so how do you know that you were at the sports hall? Did someone tell you that's where you were?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you that I tried to look through that small hole and I could see a little bit. We could find that out once we arrived, because the others were there -- the other Muslims from Mahala were there. There were five or six truckloads of them when we arrived to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You didn't ever try to look out again because you said that they would -- that one time you looked out, they tried to hit you. Did you ever try to make an opening in the canvas while the truck was actually driving?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once a young man tried to do that, but they stopped him and told him, "If you try again --" a reserve policeman said that if he tried it again, that we would all be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But were there guards riding on the outside of the canvas or something?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were in trucks, and there was a Golf escorting them with the policeman Dosenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During the time you were in Manjaca, were the people who were confined there with you wearing military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So they were wearing their own clothing?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They received some old uniforms in the other camp, those that had come earlier before us, a month before us. And my brother, when I saw him for the first time, he had a grey winter shirt and slacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That were a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was bronze in colour. It was not the olive-grey colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that during the time you were at Manjaca you and several of the over people -- most of the other people there lost quite a large amount of weight; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the clothes that you came there in probably didn't fit you very well by the time you left there. Would that be a reasonable conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When was it that the ICRC gave jackets to everybody there? Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was December 13th in the evening, the day before we were to leave a number of prisoners --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first group of 1.400 prisoners. These were warm jackets, winter jackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What colour were they?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of different colours. Blue, red, different colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. There also was a time, wasn't there, when the ICRC arranged for you to get shoes.

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before, yes. Before we left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall ever getting any kiwis to eat?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Red Cross started feeding us. It was towards the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That last day, as you were leaving Manjaca, were you all at one point standing outside the camp, lined up outside the camp getting ready to board vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before, on the 13th, there was a roll call and 50 people were appointed to board the trucks. There were groups of 50. That was the preparation. And the next day we boarded the trucks in groups of 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And right before you boarded those trucks -- well, the first thing, I want to ask you this: There were some representatives from international organisations present on that day, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And right before you boarded those trucks, did any of the prisoners who were leaving make any speeches?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of the prisoners held speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were yesterday shown a document by counsel signed by Stojan Zupljanin which referenced the bombing of your house in Sanski Most. Do you remember that? You don't need to look for it now, but do you remember you were shown that document?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, although that report was made, you said in your statement to the OTP -- and I'm reading from page 3 of the English translation -- "I should not even have reported it," speaking about the bombing of your house, "as there is no investigation and they never did anything about it." My question is: Are you aware of anybody being arrested and even prosecuted for bombing the homes or businesses of Muslims in Sanski Most in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know that anyone was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In 1992, did you own a car or a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a Lada 1300 special.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What happened to that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left it in Caplje with my mother-in-law, and then after I found her she told me that some soldiers had come and taken the car. She tried to stop them, but she couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked today about what happened when a transport truck that you were on on July 7th arrived at Manjaca. And you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. said that Spaga, who you saw as a person -- the warden, the person in charge of the camp, came out and said that only people who could walk would be admitted, or words to that effect. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, other than providing some water to try to wake up or help these men who were in such bad shape that they couldn't walk, did the camp command provide any other medical assistance to these people who couldn't walk who were being delivered to their care?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were taken inside, and they stayed behind. And I don't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were also asked -- or there was a conversation about how the food or the kitchens were the same for the guards in the camp and for the prisoners. Well, did you notice whether any of the guards had difficulties standing up and became light-headed the way that you described that you and your fellow prisoners were at the beginning because of lack of food?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter made a mistake. It wasn't the guards. It was the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you -- let me -- let me phrase the question myself in a way which hopefully you will be able to understand. You are a hundred per cent right. You had actually stated that it was fellow prisoners who in the beginning were light-headed and would need time to stand on their two feet because of lack of food. The question of

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS WAS
utterances.text: "Were any of the guards that you could see -- that you could observe in the same condition, or was it just the prisoners that were in that condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned only the prisoners. I never saw a single guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to clear up one point that counsel asked you about. He asked you about -- excuse me one moment. I'm looking at page 4 of the English translation of your statement. You don't need the statement in front of you for this question. He asked you about your brother Jasmin and a young Muslim man being called out and being placed in front of a transporter vehicle and used as human shields. Now, whose transporter vehicle was that? In other words, was that a transporter vehicle of the army, the SOS, or a different group? Could you tell me ...?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a vehicle used by the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about this court document -- about the death certificate in which you appeared as a witness in that hearing at Sanski Most. In your statement to us, to the Office of the Prosecutor, you wrote that Mirhat Delic died on that transport and that he made this gurgling sound as he died. Do you have any doubt in your mind that Mirhad, Mirhat, however you -- you said you didn't know how to spell his first name -- that Mirhad Delic died on that transport that you were on? Is there any doubt about that in your mind?

utterances.speaker: BEKIR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he died. And to this day nothing is known. They are registered as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. There are no questions from the Bench. And that means, Mr. Delic, that your task here is over, your testimony has come to an end. And on behalf of the Tribunal, it is my duty to thank you for having come over to give your evidence here in this trial. You will now be escorted out of this courtroom by the usher, and you will be given all the attention you require in preparation for the return of yourself to where you came from. I thank you once more. And should you need anything between now and your return, please get in touch with the persons responsible from the Victims and Witnesses Section. I thank you. You may now withdraw. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we'll have a break now. The next witness is in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. He is not in closed session, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's a protective --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Certain protective measures were granted, pseudonym and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we will need to prepare the room, because he needs to come in when the curtains are drawn, because otherwise --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Judge, I will take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will take care of that. Madam Registrar, I thank you. So we will resume at 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very soon you will be starting your evidence here in this Tribunal and in this particular case. And before you do so, I want to put your mind at rest, set your mind at rest, that the protective measures that you asked for have been granted and are being observed. You will not be referred to by your name, but you have been given a number and we will be referring to you as BT16. You are a number. Also you have asked for image distortion, and that mean that is no one will be able to see you as you appear to us in this courtroom. No one, in other words, outside of this courtroom will be able to see your face because your image will be distorted. Having said that, there is only one other thing that I need to tell you, and that is that it is the practice of this Tribunal that before you start giving evidence, you enter a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will tell us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. It's the equivalent of an oath in any jurisdiction that you may be familiar with. The text of the solemn declaration is contained on a piece of paper which the usher standing next to you is holding in her hands. She's going to give it to you now. Please stand up and read that solemn declaration aloud. That would be your undertaking before this Tribunal to tell us the truth and the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and you may sit down. I'll explain briefly where you are and who we are. We are the three judges composing this Trial Chamber. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Agius and I come from Malta. To my right I have Judge Janu from the Czech Republic, and to my left Judge Taya from Japan. The three persons you see to your right in the front row are the members of the team of the Prosecutor. They are handling the Prosecution in this case. And the lady in the middle will be the officer from the -- the high officer from the Prosecution that will put questions to you in direct examination. When that is over, it will be the turn of the two Defence teams to cross-examine you. This is a right, a fundamental right, which is reserved not only by our Rules of Procedure and by our Statute but also by the most fundamental of -- rules of international law. You will be examined by the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin, which is in the front row to your left the three persons that you see, and in the back row always to your left there is the Defence team for General Momir Talic, and they, too, will be cross-examining you. When we come to that stage there will be something else that I will need to tell you. For the time being, please concentrate your attention to the questions that the Prosecution will be putting forward -- putting to you, and try in your answers to be brief and precise. The secret in giving a good testimony is to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. If you deviate from that, you will be kept here longer, your stay will become longer and longer, and you will get tired, and we will get tired, and no one will be pleased. So Madam Richterova, please you may proceed with your first question in examination-in-chief

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I ask the usher to show you a piece of paper. Read it for yourself, and state only whether yes or no it is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Please show it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please show it to the Defence and to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit number P846 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were born in Sanski Most but you lived in the village of Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness approach the microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Richterova, my attention is being drawn to the transcript. Although we -- I personally heard the witness say Bosniak, there is no reported reply to your question "Witness, what is your nationality?" Sir, am I correct in saying that you answered Bosniak to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead, Ms. -- Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You answered you lived in the village of Hrustovo. And we know that the village of Hrustovo is comprised of several hamlets. Which part of Hrustovo did you live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: I lived in the hamlet of Handanovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic composition of this hamlet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: It was purely Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness a map which was previously exhibited under P803. However, these maps were annotated by previous witnesses, so I would like to provide a copy which hasn't been annotated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I didn't catch it, but there's got to be a mistake, I would think, in line 14 up near the top of your screen," what is your religion?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, he's apparently converted, because in his statement to the OTP he says he's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what he answered. I know that that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you a Catholic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can anyone explain to me how on earth -- what did you answer when you were asked the question "What is your religion?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can anyone explain to me how answering I am a Muslim becomes I am a Catholic? Anyway, I'm -- for the record, I did hear "Catholic," and the other two Judges are confirming that they, too, heard him -- not him, heard the interpreter say that he was Catholic -- that he answered that he was a Catholic. We have not converted you as yet. So for the record, it will now go that you are confirming that you are a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So this will be Exhibit P803.2. Can we place it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you show on this map where the hamlet Handanovici is approximately, because it is not printed on this map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you please take a highlighter and mark it as "H."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Richterova. My attention is being -- let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are in open session, Madam Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to leave this map on the ELMO, but I am not referring to this map right now but in the future. So we can leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You lived in your village in 1992. How would you describe general situation in the area of your village and the surrounding areas in 1992, or better, say, in the first half of the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: The situation was such that it was tense. And on the media we were able to see that in some parts of our country of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the war had already started and we were all very much afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your village did you stood any guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were these guards armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Partly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the purpose of these guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: The purpose was simply because we were afraid that somebody might catch us by surprise. Guard duty was mostly at night. We didn't want what happened later to happen to us then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, I was talking about the guards in your village, which was a Muslim village. Are you aware whether there were also guards in village which were occupied by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, but probably there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the 1992, are you aware of any checkpoints in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you be more specific and tell us where these checkpoints were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: The checkpoints were to be found at almost all the main crossroads between the main road running from Kljuc to Sanski Most, then in the town itself, on the approaches to the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you personally went through any of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Some were manned by reservists, some by the police, and there was one with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you are talking about reservists, can you be again more specific. Whom do you refer as reservists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: The reservists are people who were civilians until a few days before that. Then they were mobilised and dressed as soldiers. Mostly Serbs, from the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was your experience when you passed these checkpoints? Were you identified? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: When they stopped us, we first had to get out of a car, if we were in a car. Then we had to show our documents, our ID card or passport or driving licence. Once I even had to put -- lean my hands against the roof of the car while they searched us, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, does this same procedure applied to Serbs who passed through these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1992 were there any -- any military presence either in your village or in surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1992 did you heard any announcements relating to hand over weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Yes. I heard on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you hear on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: We heard that the Muslim population of the villages of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje had to hand over the weapons that they owned, that they could go to Tomina, a neighbouring village, that nothing would happen to them, and if they didn't do that then they would begin to shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will go back to my previous question for a second. You stated there was an army in Sanski Most. Are you aware which unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that there were soldiers and not the army in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are right, Madam Fauveau. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah. That they -- soldiers in Sanski Most. And he said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say that there was an army in Sanski Most or that there were soldiers -- that there were the military in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know which unit these soldiers belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: Mostly the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How did you learn that they belonged to 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: They are inhabitants of Sanski Most who a couple of months earlier were civilians. As a result of the mobilisation, they developed into the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Have you heard from some other sources which unit was stationed in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT16
utterances.text: I learnt it from the people who were living there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
